transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-12
Start time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Marta Chen (NovaHealth Head of ML), Evan Brooks (NovaHealth Platform), Dr. Sameer Patel (NovaHealth Lead DS)

Summary:
Short walkthrough of Redwood Optimize console focused on quantization profiles (INT8 vs FP8), mapping of fidelity degradation across output classes, and decision heuristics for fallback rules and SLA alignment. Agreed to run a sandbox benchmark on NovaHealth sample prompts and follow up with sensitivity results.

Topics covered:
- Quick overview of Optimize and how profiles are applied per-route
- INT8 vs FP8 tradeoffs, where each makes sense in NovaHealth workloads
- Fidelity degradation mapping: how we measure and visualize drop-offs per intent
- Canary / rollout strategies and automatic fallback thresholds
- Security and audit concerns for healthcare data (SOC2, KMS, VPC options)
- Next steps and pilot logistics

Action items (auto-summary):
- Redwood: run sensitivity sweep and share metrics CSV + plots
- NovaHealth: provide representative prompts and target acceptance thresholds
- Redwood: share pricing options for a 3-month pilot on Dedicated capacity

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan with Redwood, I'm the AE on this account. We also have Priya from the SE team who will do the deep dive. Marta, Evan, Sameer, thanks for making time.
[00:18] Marta: Yep thanks, excited to see how the quant profiles look with our notes. We have a few quick constraints — low latency for triage, but can't lose diagnostic fidelity for downstream clinicians.
[00:30] Priya: Totally, and that's exactly what we wanted to map today — show the Optimize console, run through the fidelity degradation map so you can see per-class regressions when moving from FP16-ish baselines to INT8 or FP8 variants.
[00:45] Evan: Quick logistic, do you need our dataset up front or can we run a sandbox? We prefer a sandbox run first.
[00:52] Jordan: Sandbox is great — we can either ingest a small sample or you can run the Redwood-provided benchmark script in your VPC. For HIPAA-sensitive stuff we usually do the sandbox inside the customer's VPC or with tokenized data.
[01:08] Sameer: Tokenized is fine — we'll scrub PHI and send, but we want fidelity mapping at the intent level — like triage vs note drafting vs coding suggestions.
[01:20] Priya: Perfect. I'll show the fidelity mapping visualization then we'll look at per-token latency and end-to-end SLO implications.
[02:05] Priya: Okay opening Optimize — so this is the profiles screen. You can see we attach profiles to routes, and each profile has precision, batch targets, and fallback rules. The UI will show historical tradeoffs for latency and quality. Note, sometimes the transcript shows this as "optima console" in the logs — ignore that, it's the same.
[02:35] Marta: Can you show the heatmap you mentioned earlier? We want to see which classes break first under INT8.
[02:42] Priya: Sure, toggling the fidelity map — here you can pick baseline FP16 output, then compare INT8 and FP8. You'll see rows for intents and columns for the metrics we track: BLEU-ish similarity, semantic similarity score, hallucination rate, and a clinician-relevance pass rate which you can set.
[03:05] Priya: For NovaHealth's triage prompts, what we usually see is: INT8 tends to hold up for short templates and classification-like outputs, but for long generative note drafting FP8 keeps fidelity higher with only a small latency hit.
[03:28] Sameer: When you say "hallucination rate" how do you compute that? Is that an internal Redwood eval or do we bring our own rubric?
[03:36] Priya: We have a baseline internal scorer using semantic similarity and a hallucination detector; you can also import your own labeled set and we'll compute the degradation relative to your labels. That's critical — the absolute numbers matter more if we compute against NovaHealth's ground truth.
[03:55] Evan: What about KV cache behavior? We saw mixed results on our side when cache warming was inconsistent.
[04:02] Priya: Good callout — KV cache warming can amplify perceived regressions. In the console you can toggle whether you simulate cold-starts versus warmed KV cache. INT8 sometimes hurts warm-cache throughput less, but cold-start latency can be worse depending on kernel availability. We call out kernel matches in the profile details.
[04:35] Jordan: From a product perspective we expose the kernel compatibility and expected latency distributions so you can set SLOs per route. If a profile is too risky we recommend a canary with an automatic fallback to FP16 or higher precision variant.
[04:52] Marta: Can you show an example of the automatic fallback config?
[04:57] Priya: Yep — in the profile you can set thresholds like "if semantic-sim drop > 0.08 or hallucination delta > 0.02 then fallback to FP8; if still failing then fallback to FP16". You can also set max allowed latency increase, e.g., don't accept >20% latency increase or fallback.
[05:20] Sameer: Are those thresholds applied live or only during canary windows?
[05:24] Priya: They can be applied either. Typical pattern: stage thresholds in a canary for 24-72 hours and then enable globally. The console keeps a changelog and you can revert.
[05:36] Evan: You said fallback to FP8 then FP16; what about a separate model variant? We sometimes prefer a smaller architecture for cost reasons.
[05:44] Priya: Absolutely — fallback can be to another model (a smaller family) or to a higher-precision version of the same model. The routing layer supports model variants by label; the console will display cost delta and latency delta for each fallback path.
[06:02] Jordan: We should also highlight the cost/latency view. Priya can pull up the per-token cost and per-request latency buckets.
[06:10] Priya: Opening the cost view — here's a comparison: baseline (FP16-ish) vs INT8 vs FP8 for a 512-token average. INT8 reduces per-token compute by ~2.3x on our measured kernels, FP8 is usually around 1.6x but retains higher fidelity on long outputs.
[06:34] Marta: So for our triage flow — likely short responses — INT8 might be best. For clinician-facing notes FP8?
[06:41] Priya: That's the usual split. The console makes it easy to apply different profiles per-route, so you don't have to pick one for everything.
[06:49] Sameer: Can you show the fidelity degradation map for a long-form note?
[06:55] Priya: Yup, pulling the long-form sample — here's FP16 baseline then INT8 comparison: you can see the semantic similarity drops around the sections with medical abbreviations and nested reasoning. The FP8 map shows much smaller drop in those segments.
[07:22] Marta: Is that because FP8 uses per-block scaling or different quantization scheme?
[07:27] Priya: It's a mix — FP8 on our runtime is implemented with preserved exponent ranges and a per-layer scaling scheme that helps with rare token distributions like medical terms. INT8 is more aggressive and can lose those tail tokens.
[07:44] Evan: Any risk of overheating GPUs with FP8 kernels? We run sustained loads.
[07:50] Priya: FP8 can be a little heavier per-way but in practice it reduces overall throughput cost while keeping latency similar. We provide recommended autoscaling curves for each precision profile for Dedicated pools.
[08:05] Jordan: Let's jump to the sandbox plan — how would we run this end-to-end?
[08:10] Priya: Two options: 1) we ingest a 2–10k sample in a Redwood sandbox we manage with tokenized records, or 2) you run our benchmark harness in your VPC and we pull logs. For HIPAA, option 2 is more common.
[08:26] Marta: We'll prefer option 2. What's required from our side?
[08:29] Priya: Just run the Python harness, point to the sample prompts file, and provide a small ground-truth label file for the intents you care about. We'll provide the script and a config example.
[08:40] Sameer: Will the harness compute clinician-relevance automatically? We want the weighted pass/fail by section.
[08:46] Priya: We have a built-in clinician-relevance module but it's easiest if you provide a small labeled set for calibration. We can then compute weighted degradation and show plots per-section.
[09:02] Jordan: I'll send the harness and a checklist after this call.
[09:06] Evan: On security, what's the approach to KMS? We need customer-managed keys and audit logging.
[09:12] Priya: We support KMS integration and HSM for Private deployments. For Hosted, we provide envelope encryption and you can bring your own key with limited access. Audit logs are available in the Console and can be forwarded to your SIEM.
[09:30] Marta: Is RBAC granular enough to separate sandbox operators from production?
[09:33] Priya: Yes — role sets separate sandbox, deploy, and billing views. We can map to your SSO via SAML/SCIM.
[09:40] Sameer: Back to the fidelity numbers — can we threshold by clinician-acceptable bounds rather than raw similarity? We have proprietary scoring for that.
[09:49] Priya: Yep, you can upload a custom metric mapping and set it as the controlling metric for rollouts. The console will then use that metric for the automatic fallback rules.
[10:05] Jordan: Quick interruption — someone in the transcript might show as "Speaker 4" sometimes, that's Fireflies artifact.
[10:12] Marta: No worries. Could we get an example CSV from a previous customer so we see the columns?
[10:18] Priya: Sure — I'll attach a sanitized sample CSV with columns: prompt_id, baseline_score, int8_score, fp8_score, delta, hallucination_delta, clinician_pass_rate.
[10:30] Sameer: We want to weight hallucinations higher than small semantic diffs. Can that be baked into the visualization?
[10:37] Priya: Yes, the visualization supports a weighted score. You can set a weight vector and the heatmap will recompute.
[11:05] Priya: I'm going to demo a quick canary config.
[11:12] Priya: Step 1: create profile -> choose INT8 -> set batch targets -> set canary percent (we usually start at 5%) -> set metric thresholds -> set fallback path. You can also pin a model version to keep deterministic behavior.
[11:35] Marta: For step-downs, what about partial fallbacks — e.g., if certain user types require higher fidelity?
[11:43] Priya: You can route by token or by user segment — profile assignment is rule-based; if the requestor is in the clinician group the route can pin to FP8 or FP16.
[11:54] Evan: How do you measure longitudinal drift? We want alerts if quality drops after a model update.
[12:00] Priya: Optimize ties back into the evaluation harness — we keep historical prompt sets and run nightly regressions. If a model update causes a delta beyond your configured alert threshold we send regression alerts and can automatically pause a rollout.
[12:20] Marta: That’s great. Can you show the historical regression UI?
[12:24] Priya: Here — timeline shows releases and per-metric deltas. You can click a release and see per-prompt breakdown.
[12:35] Sameer: On the rollout pause, is that automatic or manual?
[12:38] Priya: You can set automatic pause rules or manual only, depends on your governance preference.
[12:45] Jordan: Let's pivot to real numbers — Priya, can you pull an example from a healthcare customer (sanitized) showing latency and fidelity across precisions?
[12:52] Priya: Pulling that chart — here's a sanitized case: for a 300-token average workload: FP16 latency P95 220ms, FP8 P95 185ms, INT8 P95 140ms. Fidelity delta (weighted metric) FP8 vs FP16: 0.03, INT8 vs FP16: 0.11. Meaning INT8 shows larger drop for this workload.
[13:20] Marta: Those deltas seem significant. We need to understand per-section impact because a small delta might be concentrated on rare but critical tokens.
[13:28] Priya: Exactly, that's why we show per-token and per-intent breakdowns. In that case the hallucination delta was concentrated on diagnostic mention spans.
[13:40] Evan: On Dedicated capacity, do you expose the same profiles?
[13:44] Priya: Yes, profiles are a control-plane abstraction; whether you're on Hosted, Dedicated, or Private the behavior is similar. The difference is autoscaling and kernel availability — Dedicated pools can be tuned to favor certain kernels for stability.
[14:00] Sameer: If we run the pilot, what's the expected timeline to have actionable results?
[14:04] Jordan: Typically sample run + sweep takes 1–2 weeks depending on how fast you provide prompts. We'll aim for results within 7 business days after you provide the sample.
[14:15] Marta: Good. For the internal stakeholders, can we get a short one-pager summarizing tradeoffs?
[14:21] Jordan: We'll include that in the follow-up email — tradeoffs, suggested profile splits (triage INT8, notes FP8), and cost delta.
[14:30] Priya: I want to surface an edge case — quantization sometimes interacts poorly with prompt engineering that relies on subtle tokenization. If your prompts contain unusual spacing or special characters, INT8 can exacerbate small prediction differences.
[14:48] Sameer: We'll flag the prompt engineering team to normalize tokens.
[14:52] Jordan: Another point — our console also supports run-time diagnostic traces you can attach to a request when debugging a regression. Those traces are bounded to a single request and scrubbed.
[15:05] Marta: Do traces contain log tokens? We are wary of any PHI.
[15:10] Priya: We can configure tracing to exclude payloads or to hash tokens. For the sandbox we'll do token hash only.
[15:22] Evan: Cost modeling question — is the cost delta linear with token count across precisions?
[15:27] Priya: Largely yes, but there are fixed overheads and kernel inefficiencies at certain lengths. The console shows per-token and per-request breakdowns so you can simulate at your real request size distribution.
[15:40] Jordan: Let's switch to a quick live demo of a sensitivity sweep we ran earlier (sanitized).
[15:46] Priya: Running the sweep now — it iterates over INT8/FP8 and computes delta metrics. You can see a table with prompt_id, baseline, int8, fp8, weighted_delta. There's also a visualization called "degradation waterfall" that shows cumulative impact ordered by worst delta.
[16:12] Marta: That waterfall is useful — would we be able to export the top 100 worst prompts for manual review?
[16:18] Priya: Yes, exportable CSV and you can annotate within the Console.
[16:25] Sameer: Could we then feed those annotations back into a retraining loop or a prompt-filtering rule?
[16:31] Priya: You can use the annotated set as part of a fine-tuning or filtering rule; Redwood offers integration points for retraining pipelines.
[16:40] Evan: Regarding model versions, how do you handle model binary compatibility when we pin an older version?
[16:46] Priya: Pinning a version ensures the same weights and kernel mapping. The Console keeps the model manifest and you can see the exact kernel/compilation used.
[16:55] Marta: If we want to prioritize low tail latency for triage we'd likely set INT8 but with a fallback to FP8 if semantic-delta spikes. Is that easy to implement?
[17:04] Priya: Absolutely — create a triage route with INT8 profile and set the rule: if weighted_delta > 0.07 or hallucination_delta > 0.01 then fallback to FP8. Canary at 5% for 48 hours.
[17:17] Jordan: We'll attach an example profile in the follow-up.
[17:22] Sameer: On observability, can we get token-level cost per request in the logs for chargeback?
[17:27] Priya: Yes, token-level billing metadata is part of the logs and can be exported to your billing system.
[17:35] Marta: A quick procurement question — what contractual SLAs are available for Dedicated pilot?
[17:40] Jordan: For Dedicated we offer a pilot SLA at 99.5% with target latency tiers. For production we'd discuss a higher SLA depending on commit. The pricing doc I'll send has details.
[17:52] Evan: Are there default autoscaling policies you recommend? Our traffic is spiky during morning rounds.
[17:58] Priya: Use predictive scaling with a short cooldown for triage routes and a more conservative policy for long-form routes. We can tune based on historical traffic patterns.
[18:10] Marta: Any gotchas when moving from sandbox to production with profiles?
[18:15] Priya: Two main ones — data distribution shift (so ensure your sample is representative) and kernel differences when a different GPU family is used in production. We flag kernel mismatches in the console.
[18:29] Sameer: If kernel mismatch exists, do you automatically recompile?
[18:33] Priya: We can recompile and ship variants, but that can add time. For Dedicated we'd recommend selecting a GPU family to ensure kernel determinism.
[18:44] Jordan: We have about 40 minutes left — any deep-dive requests?
[18:49] Marta: Can we test a live failover scenario and see the behavior in the console?
[18:54] Priya: Yes, let's trigger a simulated canary failure. (short pause) Simulating now — console shows canary percent rising, then we inject metric failure and watch the automatic fallback execute. You can see request traces rerouted to FP8 and alerts created.
[19:22] Evan: Nice — can those alerts be forwarded to PagerDuty?
[19:26] Priya: Yep, we have integrations for PagerDuty, Slack, and email.
[19:32] Sameer: On the alert content, will it include the top failing prompts?
[19:36] Priya: Alerts include a summary and a link to the per-prompt breakdown; you can configure attachments.
[19:45] Jordan: I'll pause for a sec — any questions on the decision heuristics?
[19:50] Marta: Just one — in cost sensitivity, is the FP8 delta always smaller than INT8?
[19:54] Priya: Not always — sometimes INT8 has better perf and acceptable fidelity; it's workload dependent. The sensitivity sweep will tell you.
[20:05] Marta: Ok. Let's talk timeline and responsibilities.
[20:09] Jordan: Proposed: NovaHealth provides 10k sample prompts + labels by 2026-11-18; Redwood runs sweep and returns results by 2026-11-25; follow-up call week of 2026-11-29 to decide pilot scope.
[20:23] Marta: That's feasible. We'll coordinate internally.
[20:27] Evan: I'll own running the harness in our VPC.
[20:30] Sameer: I'll curate the label set.
[20:33] Priya: Great — I'll send the harness and a sanitized example CSV.
[20:38] Jordan: Anything else on security?
[20:41] Marta: Just to confirm — audit logs retention and export?
[20:44] Priya: Audit logs can be retained for configurable windows and exported to your S3 or SIEM. For Private deployments retention can be much longer.
[20:56] Jordan: Alright, quick recap of next steps and we'll close.
[21:00] Jordan: (recap) Priya will run the sensitivity sweep after you provide prompts; Jordan will send pricing and pilot options; NovaHealth will provide prompts and labels; schedule follow-up post-results.
[21:20] Marta: Sounds good, thanks.
[21:24] Evan: Thanks all.
[21:26] Sameer: Thanks.
[21:30] Jordan: Bye everyone.
